segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: if indeed you have heard of the administration of God’s grace that was given to me for you:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: by revelation the secret was made known to me, as I wrote above in brief.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the secret of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the good news,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: of which I became a servant according to the gift of God’s grace, given to me according to the working of his power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To me, less than the least of all the holy ones, this grace was given: to bring the Gentiles the good news of the unfathomable riches of Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to enlighten everyone as to what is the administration of the secret hidden for ages in God, who created all things,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that the richly varied wisdom of God might now be made known through the assembly to the rulers and the authorities in the heavenly places,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in keeping with the purpose of the ages that he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I ask you not to lose heart at my afflictions on your behalf, which are your glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason I bend my knees before the Father,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: from whom every family in the heavens and on earth takes its name,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, and that you, rooted and grounded in love,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: may be strong enough to grasp, with all the holy ones, what is the breadth and length and height and depth,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled to all the fullness of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now to him who is able to do beyond everything, far more than all we ask or conceive, according to the power at work in us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus, to all the generations of the age of the ages. Amen.

notes.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'; in the plural it was the ordinary Jewish way of referring to all the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant, but it is one Greek word throughout.

notes.phrase: For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles—
notes.traditional: For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles,
notes.note: The sentence has no main verb and breaks off. Most interpreters think Paul digresses in verses 2–13 and resumes at verse 14, where 'For this reason' is repeated. A minority supply a verb here: 'I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus.'

The word means the management of a household or estate, and by extension an arrangement or a task of management. Here it may be the responsibility entrusted to Paul ('stewardship', 'commission') or the way God has arranged for his grace to be dispensed ('plan'). The same word recurs in verse 9, where God's arrangement is more clearly in view; 'administration' is used in both places to keep the link visible.

In the period, and especially in the Greek version of Daniel, this word means a secret, in particular a purpose of God that is hidden until he discloses it. 'Mystery' now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul's point is that the secret has been revealed and can be stated plainly (verse 6). Most translations keep 'mystery', usually explaining it in this sense.

The Greek word was an ordinary term for good tidings, such as news of a victory or a ruler's accession. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and remains common. 'Good news' is used here because it carries the plain sense and keeps the link with the related verb in verse 8, 'to bring … the good news'.

The word refers to all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people' or 'his holy people'.

A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation; it should not be heard as a single meeting.

notes.traditional: by the faith of him; through faith in him
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'through the faith of him'. The majority reading takes this as faith directed toward Christ. A substantial number of scholars read it as Christ's own faithfulness: 'through his faithfulness'. The grammar allows either.

notes.phrase: I ask you not to lose heart
notes.traditional: I desire that ye faint not
notes.note: The Greek names neither the person asked nor who might lose heart. Most take it as a request to the readers not to be discouraged by Paul's imprisonment. It could also be a prayer to God that the readers not lose heart or, less probably, that Paul himself not lose heart.

The Greek word for a family or clan (patria) is formed from the word for father (patēr), so a hearer caught a link with 'the Father' in the previous verse that English cannot reproduce. The word means a group descended from a common ancestor, not 'fatherhood' in the abstract. The older rendering 'the whole family' is unlikely without the article in Greek.
The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that this translation keeps wherever it occurs. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'.

In the Greek, 'in love' stands between the clause about Christ dwelling in their hearts and the words 'rooted and grounded', and could belong to either. The edition translated here punctuates it with what precedes: 'that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, in love'. Most translations and commentators attach it to 'rooted and grounded', as here; the punctuation is editorial and not part of the ancient text.

notes.phrase: to all the generations of the age of the ages
notes.traditional: throughout all ages, world without end; throughout all generations, for ever and ever
notes.note: The Greek piles up time expressions in a Semitic style: literally 'to all the generations of the age of the ages'. The phrase is an emphatic way of saying 'for all time without end', and most translations paraphrase it so. The literal form is kept here because the letter has spoken repeatedly of 'the ages' (verses 9 and 11).

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation; 'mystery' and 'secret' give readers quite different impressions and the choice should be uniform.
Very frequent noun with a cognate verb (εὐαγγελίζομαι, v. 8); 'gospel' versus 'good news' must be settled once so noun and verb stay linked across books.
Used of both Paul's stewardship and God's plan (Eph 1:10; 3:2, 9; Col 1:25; 1 Cor 9:17); translators vary between stewardship, commission, plan and administration.
Appears in 'this age', 'from the ages' and the doxological 'to the ages of the ages'; a policy is needed on when to keep 'age' and when to use 'forever' or 'eternal'.
Common across the New Testament and rendered variously as tribulation, affliction, trouble, suffering or distress; a single default would keep the thread visible.
